title: T38 (exploratory): E2 recalibration on the smoke run, with a leave-one-out check
body:
**What this does:**
The recalibration part of T38, on the only E2 checker outputs that exist: the 10 smoke-run patients (#49), rebuilt from the committed `results/e2_smoke/rule_table.csv` (CPU only, no new model run). Code: `trialguide.eval.e2_recalibration`; write-up with caveats first: `results/e2_recalibration/README.md`.

**Result:** with 10 patients the smallest certifiable target is 9.1%, so **alpha 5% and 2% cannot be certified** (the policy would accept no inference toward eligibility); at alpha 10%, lambda-hat = **0.992** against the main run's 0.766. In-sample (170 unsettled rules): accepting everything gives 6 harmful of 91 accepted (4.0%); the frozen 0.766 gives 5 of 89 (3.8%), so it filters almost nothing on E2 notes; the recalibrated 0.992 gives 1 of 71 (0.4%), at about a fifth fewer accepted inferences. Leave-one-out (fit on 9, apply to the 10th): 0 harmful of 69 accepted, against 5 of 89 at the frozen threshold.

**Please do not over-read it:** only 6 harmful inferences exist in the whole run; the reference is the checker on the full note (model-derived, E2 has no expert labels); there is no held-out E2 set (the E2 test half stays sealed), so the in-sample numbers are optimistic; and the strict threshold is partly mechanical (with n = 10 the correction alone uses 9.1 of the 10 points). It fits the proposal's warning that a threshold does not carry over to different patients, but as a hint, not a result.

**For you (Prakash):** README untouched. If you mention it: 'E2 recalibration was run only as an exploratory check on 10 smoke-run patients (model-derived reference, no held-out set); with 10 patients the 5% target cannot be certified, and the 10% target gives a much stricter threshold (0.992) than the main run's 0.766; see `results/e2_recalibration/`'.

title: T38 (exploratory): E2 smoke run on 10 Indian-affiliated case reports
body:
**What this does:**
A small, **exploratory** version of T38. The planned E2 evaluation (the full system on the 100 E2 patients, with recalibration on the 50 calibration patients) did not fit the time and compute left, so this checks that the frozen system runs on Indian-affiliated case reports and gives a first look at how it behaves. Code: `trialguide.eval.e2_smoke` (runner, summary, and a `--merge` command for the per-GPU parts); results and caveats: `results/e2_smoke/README.md`; Kaggle script: `scripts/kaggle/t38_e2_smoke/`.

**Setup:** 10 seeded patients from the E2 **calibration** half (the E2 test half was never opened); the top 2 of the 157 E2 trials per patient by BM25 (355 rules, the same for the full and the masked note); frozen commit `55be3fe`, Qwen3-8B 8-bit greedy, 40% rule-targeted masking, Kaggle 2 x T4 (78 min). B6, B2 and B5 on the same checks. **No doctor, no B7, no recalibration, no gold labels**: the reference is the checker's own judgement on the full note, as in the T45 reference check.

**Result:** the checker settles 77.5% of rules on the full note; 40% masking leaves 69% unresolved under B6. Of the 170 rules lost to masking, B2 recovers 48.8% (32.8 to 64.9), settles 4.7% wrongly and 3.5% wrongly toward eligibility; B5 (0.9) recovers 47.6%, 4.1% wrong, 2.9% toward eligibility. On the main test run the same definitions give B2 21.4% recovered, 6.4% wrong, 2.2% toward eligibility.

**Please do not read the higher recovery as "better on Indian patients".** Three reasons, all in the results README: (1) the reference is the checker itself, so where it infers "not met" from silence on both the full and the masked note, they agree and it counts as recovered; inference is 30% of checks on E2 notes against 16% on the TREC/SIGIR test notes; (2) the 10 patients were matched to only 9 distinct trials (one is a candidate for 5 patients), so many rules are trivially "not met"; (3) 10 patients, no calibration, and B5's 0.9 is not tuned for E2.

**For you (Prakash):** README results are untouched. If you mention E2, I would say: "E2 evaluation not run as planned; an exploratory smoke run on 10 calibration-half case reports (checker only, no recalibration) shows the system runs on these notes; see `results/e2_smoke/`".

**Licence note:** the raw checks contain explanations that paraphrase PMC-Patients text (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), so they are not committed; `rule_table.csv` holds every status, category and confidence without the text. The raw output is in the Kaggle notebook only.

**How I tested it:** 6 tests for the runner and the merge command (scripted checker, tiny trials); a dry run on the real E2 patients and trials with a scripted checker before any GPU use; the merge command reproduces my ad-hoc summary exactly; every figure in the results README was checked against `summary.json` and the main test run (two claims I had not yet verified were checked first). Full suite 396 pass.

title: T36: H1 and H2 verdicts and McNemar tests from the saved test run
body:
Stacked on #39 (base is the resplit branch; this diff shows only the verdicts). It needs #39's Kaggle checks for one comparison.

**What this does:**
The statistics half of T36 (Prakash's part): `trialguide.eval.verdicts` computes the H1 and H2 verdicts, with the proposal's wording, and exact McNemar tests, from the saved test run (`results/test_run/`). No model was called; I did it because the H1/H2 verdicts were not stated anywhere in the repo yet. Full tables and reading notes: `results/verdicts/README.md`.

**Result: both verdicts are inconclusive, neither hypothesis is supported.**
- **H1** (recovery of B7 at least 10 points above B4, false-eligible no higher): B7 recovers 7.6%, B4 4.4%; the **gain is +3.2 points, CI -0.1 to +10.6**. The estimate is under the target; it is "inconclusive" rather than "not supported" only because the CI's upper end (10.6) is just above 10. False-eligible is identical (70 rules each). Raw NDCG@10 difference B7 minus B4: +0.0017 [0.0000, 0.0044]. The CIs are wide because masking costs only 0.053 NDCG, so a ratio against it is unstable (4.2% of resamples fell below the 0.02 gap floor and were dropped, as the proposal specifies).
- **H2** (harmful rate within 5% and lower than B5 and an uncorrected tuned threshold): B7 is 3.93% with CI 1.25 to 7.41, so upper bound above 5% and lower bound below it: **inconclusive**. B7 is **not lower than B5** (3.93% vs 2.97%).
- **McNemar** (3,728 rules masking made B6 leave open): B7 vs B4 9 vs 4 discordant, p = 0.27; B7 vs A1 820 vs 4 (inference is what recovers rules); A6 and B3 each recover 37-38 more rules than B7.

**Worth a sentence in the report (my finding while checking):** risk control barely binds with 26 calibration patients. The conformal correction alone costs 1/27 = 3.7%, so the calibration risk may be at most about 1.35% to meet 5%, and accepting every inference already sits at 1.0 to 1.5%. That is why lambda-hat is so unstable (0.766 on the cluster, 0.562 on the Kaggle re-run) and why B7 behaves close to B2.

**Where it needed a different source:** the cluster run kept only totals, so the paired B7-vs-B5/B2/uncorrected-tuned comparison uses the per-rule Kaggle re-run from #39 (close to, but not identical with, the cluster run; stated in the README). The primary verdict uses the cluster numbers.

**Please confirm (Prakash):**
1. The false-eligible clause of H1 uses the team's rule-level definition (`eval/recovery.py`), because trial-level decisions were not saved. Say if you meant trial level.
2. "Uncorrected tuned threshold" = the smallest threshold whose *empirical* calibration risk is at most 5% (no 1/(n+1) correction).
3. I did not edit the README results; whether and how to quote these verdicts is yours.

**How I tested it:** 4 new tests (patient alignment, which rules count as lost, uncorrected threshold, verdict wiring); full suite 379 pass. Every number in the results README was checked against `verdicts.json`. Surprises were checked before writing (B7 and B4 identical false-eligible counts: they differ on 13 rules, none in that class).

**Not covered:** trial-level false-eligible and false-exclusion rates, the budget sweep, and E1/E2 verdicts.

**What this does:**
The plan has a 200-rule audit of the model-derived full-note reference (T45) and a hand check of 50 cited inferences (T44). **Neither human check was done.** This PR adds the part that can be done automatically from saved outputs: `trialguide.eval.reference_audit` compares the full-note checker's labels and cited sentences (`results/test_run/checks_full.jsonl`) with the expert labels and expert evidence sentences, with patient-level bootstrap CIs. - When the checker settles a rule the experts also settled, it is right **90.8% [83.7, 95.6]**; wrong toward eligibility on 1.2% [0.0, 3.0] of expert-settled rules.
- But it is **not a neutral reference**: it settles only 73.9% of the rules the experts settled, and it settles **57%** of the 86 rules the experts call "not enough information".

**Limits (also in the README):** only 266 of the 496 expert-labelled test rules could be matched to a checked rule (the test run covered a sample of trials per patient); expert evidence exists for SIGIR only; this is descriptive and post-hoc on saved outputs of the frozen system (nothing changed), so it supports but does not replace the human checks. Since the report can no longer claim a hand audit, this is probably the honest wording for the reference-label limitation.

**For you (Prakash):** the README's "Not run" line (my PR #37) still lists the 200-rule audit and the 50-inference hand check as not done, which stays true; this PR adds an automatic substitute and does not touch the README.

**What this does:**
Adds the exploratory resplits the proposal promises (Section 5, "repeat the calibration/test split 200 times"), my part of T36, as `trialguide.eval.resplits`, and runs them. The cluster runs kept only totals, not per-rule checks, so I re-ran the calibration and test checks on Kaggle (2 x T4, 74 minutes; kernel script in `scripts/kaggle/risk_checks/`) at the frozen commit `55be3fe`: Qwen3-8B 8-bit, greedy, tools on, 40% rule mask, same code path as `run_risk.py`.

**1. The Kaggle re-run is close but not identical to the published cluster numbers:**

| | Cluster | Kaggle |
|---|---|---|
| lambda-hat (26 cal patients) | 0.766 | **0.562** |
| Test B7 at the frozen 0.766: accepted / harmful | 46 / 11 (3.93%) | 47 / 12 (3.94%) |
| Test B2: accepted / harmful | 50 / 12 (4.11%) | 52 / 14 (4.32%) |
| Test unsettled rules | 386 | 397 |

title: T24: E2 data - Indian-affiliated oncology case reports and trials recruiting in India
body:
Stacked on the T17 PR #10 (base is the T17 branch; the diff shows only T24). Merge order: #4, #7, #8, #9, #10, then this.

**What this does:**
Builds the E2 extension data as the proposal defines it: PMC-Patients summaries whose source articles have authors at Indian institutions, oncology only, matched to trials recruiting in India, with a calibration half for recalibration.

| Step | Count |
|---|---|
| PubMed `India[ad] AND case reports[pt] AND neoplasms[majr]` | 16,085 |
| Affiliation strings re-checked for "India" | 16,041 |
| ...with a summary in PMC-Patients V1 | 346 |
| Adults (>= 18), one patient per article = **pool** | 276 |
| **Sample** (seed 20261030): `splits/e2/e2_cal.txt` / `e2_test.txt` | 50 / 50 |
| ClinicalTrials.gov recruiting, cancer condition, **an Indian site recruiting**: `e2_trials.txt` | 157 of 181 |

- `download.py --with-pmc-patients` fetches PMC-Patients V1 (545 MB, pinned HF revision, checksummed). E1 can use the same file.
- Trials are converted to the TrialGPT corpus format, so retrieval, masking and the checker run unchanged (checked: E2 notes load and mask with the T10 code).
- `load_e2_patients(Split.TEST)` raises unless `allow_test=True`.
- PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov change daily, so the committed ID lists are the dataset (hashes in `e2_info.json`); `python -m trialguide.data.e2` re-verifies them.

**Limits** are written down in `docs/e2_limits.md` (affiliation is not nationality, case reports are unusual, MeSH Neoplasms includes some benign tumours, **no gold labels**, time mismatch between old reports and current trials, notes about 3x longer than TREC/SIGIR, no CTRI, CC BY-NC-SA licence).

**Please note / confirm:**
1. **Vidur (E1, T23/T31):** `splits/e2/e1_exclude_pmids.txt` lists all 276 pool articles. E1 teacher labels and QLoRA training must skip these PMIDs, or E2 tests on training data.
2. **Adults only:** 71 of 346 articles were paediatric, but only 13 of the 157 trials accept under-18s, so children would have almost nothing to match.
3. **"Recruiting in India"** requires an Indian site whose own status is recruiting; 24 trials only had Indian sites that were not yet recruiting or closed.
4. **For T38:** E2 has no expert labels, so its evaluation needs a model-derived reference and/or a small labelled subset; recalibration uses the 50-patient E2 calibration half (smallest certifiable alpha about 2%).

**How I tested it:**

title: T17: evaluation harness (NDCG@10, recovery, false-eligible/exclusion, bootstrap, McNemar)
body:
Stacked on the T10 PR #9 (base is the T10 branch; the diff shows only T17). Merge order: #4, #7, #8, #9, then this. It really only needs the T8 split, so it can be re-based onto T8 if that is easier.

**What this does:**
`trialguide.eval` computes the proposal's headline numbers from per-patient system outputs:
- `ranking.py`: NDCG@10 and graded P@10 with TrialGPT's conventions; gold grades from the qrels (`load_gold_grades`).
- `stats.py`: paired patient-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples, 95% percentile CI, same resampled patients for every system), **recovery** as a ratio of averages (not reported when the B1-B6 gap is under 0.02, as the proposal says), exact McNemar, and `h1_verdict` / `h2_verdict` worded exactly as in the proposal.
- `decisions.py`: false-eligible and false-exclusion rates, precision/recall of "eligible", unknown rate, each with a bootstrap CI.
- `report.py`: `ranking_report(...)`, one call for NDCG@10, P@10 and recovery with CIs, for the B2/B6/B7 numbers at the progress check.

**How I tested it:**
25 new tests with hand-computed values (full suite: 77 pass). NDCG@10 and P@10 agree with Prateek's T4 `evaluate.py` on 5,000 random rankings (0 disagreements). On the real dev patients (dev only) an oracle ranking scores 1.000, an inverted one 0.000 and a random one 0.199 [0.151, 0.253]. The test split's gold labels are sealed: `load_gold_grades(Split.TEST)` raises unless `allow_test=True`.

**Please confirm (Prakash, since you consume this in T21/T36):**
1. **False-eligible / false-exclusion denominators** are my reading, the proposal does not give them: false-eligible = "eligible" decisions that are not eligible (grade 0 or 1) / all not-eligible pairs; false-exclusion = "excluded" decisions that are eligible / all eligible pairs. A system decides `eligible`, `excluded` or `unknown`; abstaining is neither error but lowers recall and raises the unknown rate. A one-function change if you meant something else.
2. **Candidate trials:** `retrieved_trials.json` is an exact subset of the qrels (0 grade disagreements), so gold comes from the qrels and only labelled pairs a system ranks are scored. `same_candidates` raises if two systems rank different trials, and a labelled trial without a score raises, so a baseline cannot silently drop hard trials.

**Still open / known limits:**
- Harmful-inference rate, coverage and the conformal loss are not here (Prakash's T30/T36, they need his accept/reject definitions). The bootstrap helpers apply to them unchanged.
- McNemar treats rules or trials as independent although they cluster within patients, so it can overstate certainty; the patient-level bootstrap is the headline.

title: T10: sentence-level facts and masking (random, rule-targeted, evidence-targeted)
body:
Stacked on the T8 PR (base is the T8 branch; the diff shows only T10). Merge order: #4, #7, #8, then this.

**What this does:**
`trialguide.data.patients` loads a split's notes and cuts them into sentence-level facts; `trialguide.data.masking` hides facts in three ways and returns a `MaskedNote` whose `.visible` (a schema `VisibleNote`) is the only thing a system may read.

- **Facts = sentences**, split with nltk exactly as TrialGPT does (plus its closing "informed consent" sentence for SIGIR). This reproduces the experts' sentence numbering for 52/52 annotated patients, so `expert_sentences` ids line up with ours.
- **random** (20/40/60%): seeded draw, at least 1 and never the whole note.
- **rule-targeted**: hides the sentences that the most candidate-trial rules ask about, scored by TF-IDF similarity (deterministic, no model, no threshold). On dev its hidden set overlaps a random 40% mask 0.47 on average (chance 0.4), so it is a genuinely different test.
- **evidence-targeted**: hides exactly the expert-cited sentences, **per patient-trial pair** by default (see below).
- Seeds are derived from (base seed, split, patient, mask type, fraction), so cal/test masks are independent of dev.
- `load_patients(Split.TEST)` raises unless `allow_test=True`, so the sealed test notes cannot be read by accident.

**Please confirm (Prakash / Prateek / Vidur):**
1. **Evidence masking is per patient-trial pair**, not per patient: the per-patient union hides a median 57% of the note, blanks 7 labelled patients completely and leaves 16 with under 2 sentences; per pair the median is 41%. Consequence: a different masked note per pair, so this mask type is scored at rule level, not with NDCG across trials. `scope="rule"` and `"patient"` also exist. It applies to the 52 expert-labelled patients (cal/test) only, not dev.
2. **Rule-targeted masking is lexical** (TF-IDF). Using the checker LLM to decide which sentences a rule needs would make the benchmark depend on the model under test; MedCPT similarity is a possible upgrade if a spot-check at the T15 pilot shows poor masks.
3. **For Vidur (T18):** `candidate_rules` reads `retrieved_trials.json`, which is for *building masks* only. Retrieval for masked runs must still use the visible note only (see `docs/leakage_checklist.md`).

**How I tested it:**
23 new tests (synthetic notes, so they run in CI; real-data checks skip when data is not downloaded): hide counts, seed independence across splits, no hidden text in the visible note, rule/evidence behaviour, the test-split guard, and the 52/52 numbering check on real data. Full suite: 52 pass. I also looked at rule vs random masks on development patients only.

**Still open / known limits:**
- A sentence can contain several facts, so hiding one hides all of them. Finer facts can be added later under the same sentence ids if the doctor or selector needs them.
- `requirements.txt` adds `nltk==3.9.2` (same version as the T4 PR); the sentence model downloads once on first use.
- Evidence statistics used to choose the pair scope were aggregated over all annotated patients, including test-split ones (dataset statistics only, nothing about the system).

body:
Stacked on the T7 PR (base is the T7 branch; the diff shows only T8). Merge order: #4, T7, T8.

**What this does:**

|---|---|---|---|---|

**Design choices to confirm (reviewer, please read):**
1. **Expert-labelled patients go to cal and test only; dev has none** (the proposal's rule, Section 6). Cost: dev has no expert rule labels, and cal/test hold ~500 labelled rules each, of which only ~3% are inference-worthy, so the 5% risk target may be infeasible on that few events. If we want ~10 labelled patients in dev, say so **before merging**: after merge the files never change.
2. **Drawn by stratified, matched-pair randomisation with seed 20261027** (the date, chosen before running, not searched): labelled patients paired by rule count with a coin flip per pair; the other 131 spread 37:47:47 per cohort. This balances gold evidence without seed hunting.
3. **Leakage finding for T18 (Vidur):** `retrieved_trials.json` stores the full note and groups trials by expert label; `id2queries.json` holds keywords from the full note. Masked runs must regenerate keywords from the visible note only and never use either file's grouping or cached keywords. Listed in `docs/leakage_checklist.md`.

title: T7: expert-label audit (coverage, NEI, recoverable NEI)
body:
Stacked on #4 (base is the T3 branch; the diff shows only T7).

**What this does:**
`trialguide.data.audit` measures what the 1,015 TrialGPT criterion annotations cover and how many "not enough information" (NEI) rules are recoverable. Output: `results/label_audit.md` and `.json` (reproduce with `python -m trialguide.data.audit`).

**Findings:**
- Usable patients (note + expert trial labels): SIGIR 58 (of 59; `sigir-201428` has no trial labels), TREC 2021 75, TREC 2022 50 = 183, matching the proposal.
- The annotation file has **1,015** rows (the dataset card agrees; the proposal's 1,020 is a typo). **All are on SIGIR patients**: 52 usable patients, 997 rows, plus 18 rows for `sigir-201426`, who appears in no cohort file. TREC has no expert rule labels.
- Expert NEI: 293 rows (28.9%). **Recoverable** (GPT-4 NEI, expert gives a definite label): 34 rows (3.3%), 21 with expert-cited evidence; 26.4% of GPT-4/expert disagreements (paper: 30.7% of 26 errors). GPT-4 over-committed (decided where expert says NEI) on 21 rows. This is a mechanical lower bound, not a hand audit.
- Consequence: natural NEI cases are rare, so rule-targeted masking (T10) must supply most infer/ask test cases.

**How I tested it:**
Hand-made dataset tests for the audit counts; the committed results reproduce byte for byte from the downloaded data.

- Expert labels exist only for SIGIR, so calibration on expert labels covers SIGIR only (see T8 for how the split handles this).

title: T19: infer / ask / abstain policy
body:
**What this does:**
Adds `src/trialguide/policy/policy.py`, the decision policy. For each rule from the checker it picks one action:
- stated → use it
- inferred toward eligibility → accept only if confidence ≥ threshold (risk control)
- inferred away from eligibility → accept (cannot be a harmful inference, D15)
- assumption / missing → question candidate, or abstain if that fact was already asked

Doctor answers follow D11: a "probably" answer is treated as an inference, and an "unsure" answer is not used as evidence and allows one follow-up. `question_candidates()` groups rules that need the same fact, and `finalize()` turns unasked questions into abstentions. `system_config()` gives B2, B5, B6, B7, A1 and A6 from one code path.

**How I tested it:**
21 unit tests in `tests/policy/test_policy.py`, all with hand-made checker outputs (no patient data). 36 tests pass in total.
